Senses.Explanation: A small convocation is a scheduled public address by the monastery's presiding master, announced to the community and delivered from the seat, but without one fixed room. The institutional code says plainly that “the small convocation initially has no fixed place” (小參初無定所): depending on the assembly's size it may use the sleeping hall (寢堂) or teaching hall (法堂). This is not a casual conversation. Its procedure begins after noon (至日午後): the attendant reports to the presiding abbot and orders the guest-office worker to notify the assembly (侍者覆住持云令客頭行者報眾), the small-convocation placard is hung (掛小參牌), the release bell is not rung that evening (當晚不鳴放參鐘), at the evening bell the worker reports again (昏鐘鳴時行者覆住持), the drum sounds once (鳴鼓一通), the assembly gathers and the two ranks take their places (眾集兩序歸位), and the presiding abbot mounts the seat and raises the guiding theme (住持登座提綱). The code names the occasions: when an abbot enters office (如住持入院), when officials or donors visit the mountain (或官員檀越入山), on a special request (或受人特請), for instruction addressed to the dead (或謂亡者開示), or at the four seasonal observances, when it is moved to the evening bell (或四節臘則移於昏鐘鳴). It says this is then called a small convocation, may recount social courtesies, “is what is called the house teaching” (曰家教者是也), and still does not sound the release bell (然亦不鳴放參鐘), “meaning that there is still convocation” (謂猶有參也). The record therefore supplies both the shorter house-teaching label (家教) and the physical ascent (登座) without turning either into a second sense. Recorded-sayings books use the same event name as a discourse heading: Dahui Zonggao's “that evening, small convocation” (當晚小參), Yuanwu Keqin's contents line “hall addresses eight; small convocations one” (卷第八　上堂八　小參一), New Year's Eve forms headed by “the last night of the year” (除夜), release and opening forms including “small convocation at opening the restraint” (結制小參), memorial and ordination forms, and Beijing Chulin Shangrui's report that the novice said “the small-convocation placard has already been hung” (已掛小參牌了也). In that address Chulin recalls asking the deputy bursar, “what is a small convocation?” and receiving “eating gruel,” then “what is a great convocation?” and receiving “eating rice” (我曾問副寺師：『如何是小參？』寺曰：『吃粥。』『如何是大參？』寺曰：『吃飯。』). Jiexian's preface lists hall address (上堂), small convocation (小參), address to the assembly (示眾), and general address (普說) as separate sections; Xingyue likewise lists evening address (晚參) alongside small convocation. They are neighboring public-address institutions, not alternate translations of one event.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 7,023 occurrences in 337 texts. The public-address institution is established by the Imperially Revised Baizhang Code (勅修百丈清規), live addresses, named occasion headings, a record's table of contents, and two independent taxonomies. Event noun, discourse heading, requested event, and the implied verb “give/hold a small convocation” are grammatical packagings of one event. No title, person, physical object, or master-specific referent was found. The code's no-fixed-place rule and special timing distinguish it from the regular hall address; the named taxonomies keep it distinct from evening address, address to the assembly, and general address.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Nominal and directive clauses prescribe venue, notification, placard, bell, drum, assembly order, and abbot duties; no historical address-giver speaks this passage.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Imperially Revised Baizhang Code (勅修百丈清規), impersonal institutional narration: the rule states that the event has no fixed place, then prescribes notification, placard, bell, drum, assembly order, and the presiding abbot's ascent. No historical speaker or address-giver is instantiated in the prescription.
